body:
Why underground resistance developed

After 9 August 1942, the British government arrested senior Congress leaders, restricted meetings and controlled the publication of political news. Openly organising a protest became increasingly difficult.

In response, some activists continued the struggle underground. This meant carrying out political activities secretly to avoid arrest and to maintain communication between participants.

Underground activity was especially important because many of the leaders who had organised earlier national movements were now in prison.

Underground movement: Political resistance conducted secretly when open organisation is prohibited or severely restricted. During Quit India, it included distributing messages, maintaining contacts and operating clandestine communication networks.

Leaders associated with underground resistance

Several leaders who were not continuously in British custody helped sustain resistance after the initial arrests.

  • Jayaprakash Narayan: A Congress Socialist leader who became a prominent organiser of underground resistance. After escaping from Hazaribagh Jail in 1942, he continued anti-colonial activities.
  • Ram Manohar Lohia: A socialist leader who participated in underground organisation and the circulation of nationalist messages.
  • Aruna Asaf Ali: After her prominent public role in August 1942, she avoided arrest and continued political activity underground.
  • Usha Mehta: A young nationalist who helped establish a secret radio service in Bombay to circulate information during the movement.

These leaders did not replace Gandhi as the movement's original leader. Their significance lies in maintaining resistance when the central Congress leadership could not organise openly.

Congress Radio: communication despite censorship

British wartime regulations imposed severe restrictions on newspapers and political communication. This made it difficult for people to obtain news of demonstrations, arrests and local resistance.

In 1942, Usha Mehta and her associates established a clandestine radio station in Bombay. It became known as Congress Radio.

The station broadcast news and nationalist messages. It used a shortwave frequency associated with a wavelength of approximately 42.34 metres. Because the broadcasts were unauthorised, the organisers kept the equipment concealed and moved the transmitting location to reduce the risk of detection.

Congress Radio helped circulate information at a time when the British controlled much of the ordinary press. It was a secret nationalist station, not a regular government broadcasting service.

The British eventually detected the operation. Usha Mehta was arrested in November 1942, bringing this phase of the clandestine broadcasting effort to an end.

Usha Mehta's Gujarat connection

Usha Mehta was born on 25 March 1920 in Saras, Gujarat. She later lived in Bombay, where she participated in nationalist activities. Her role in Congress Radio is an important link between Gujarat and the Quit India Movement.

How underground work differed from mass demonstrations

A public procession openly challenged British authority by bringing participants together in the streets. Underground activity operated through smaller networks, secret communications and concealed organisational work.

Both belonged to the wider Quit India struggle, but they were not identical methods. Underground resistance became more significant as public demonstrations were dispersed and arrests increased.

Prelims focus

  • Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia were associated with underground resistance during Quit India.
  • Aruna Asaf Ali participated in underground activity after August 1942.
  • Usha Mehta helped organise Congress Radio in Bombay.
  • Congress Radio operated during 1942 and was associated with a shortwave wavelength of 42.34 metres.
  • Usha Mehta was born in Saras, Gujarat, and was arrested in November 1942.
  • Trap: Congress Radio was a clandestine nationalist broadcast, not an official British Indian radio service.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, 'Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement', section 'Quit India', printed p. 363; Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Mumbai Legacy Project, 'Dr. Usha Mehta', pp. 1–2; Mani Bhavan Gandhi Sangrahalaya, 'Quit India, 1942', section on Congress Radio (consulted 21 November 2026); Employment News, Vol. 18, 4–10 August 2018, 'Quit India Movement: An Important Milestone in Our Struggle for Freedom', sections on censorship and underground activity; Press Information Bureau, 'Quit India Movement', 5 August 2017 (consulted 21 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Secret radio broadcasting helped circulate nationalist information during the crackdown.

title: Underground Leadership, Secret Communication and Congress Radio

body:
What was a parallel government?

During the Quit India Movement, resistance became so strong in some districts that the normal functioning of British administration was disrupted. Local nationalists attempted to establish alternative institutions to manage public affairs.

These arrangements were called parallel governments because they claimed or exercised local administrative authority in opposition to the existing colonial government.

They were not recognised as independent national governments. Their authority was limited to particular localities, and their duration varied considerably.

Parallel government: A temporary alternative administration established by local nationalist groups in an area where British colonial authority had been weakened or challenged.

Three important examples

PlacePeriodAssociated leaderImportant feature
Ballia, United Provinces, now Uttar PradeshAugust 1942Chittu PandeyShort-lived popular administration after disruption of British control
Tamluk, Midnapore, BengalDecember 1942–1944Satish Chandra SamantaTamralipta Jatiya Sarkar; local justice, security and relief work
Satara, Bombay Presidency, now MaharashtraFrom 1943 into 1946Nana Patil and other local leadersPrati Sarkar; people's courts and organised village-level resistance

Ballia: a short-lived local government

In Ballia, in the United Provinces, large-scale protests disrupted colonial administration in August 1942. On 20 August 1942, a popular government was proclaimed under Chittu Pandey.

The British soon restored their control through police and military action. Ballia is therefore remembered for a brief but significant attempt to replace colonial authority at the district level.

Tamluk: the Tamralipta Jatiya Sarkar

In the Tamluk area of Midnapore, Bengal, nationalists formed the Tamralipta Jatiya Sarkar on 17 December 1942.

Satish Chandra Samanta was a leading figure in this parallel administration. It attempted to maintain local order, administer justice and organise assistance for people facing hardship. Its activities included relief work after a destructive cyclone affected the region.

Unlike the brief experiment at Ballia, the Tamluk administration continued for an extended period, until August 1944.

Satara: the Prati Sarkar

In the Satara district of the former Bombay Presidency, nationalist groups established the Prati Sarkar, meaning a parallel or alternative government.

The movement developed strongly during 1943. Nana Patil became an important leader associated with it. Local supporters organised village units, volunteer groups and people's courts.

People's courts were institutions through which local activists attempted to settle disputes outside the normal colonial judicial system. Volunteer organisations helped sustain resistance in villages.

The Tufan Dals were village-level volunteer units associated with the Satara movement. The Prati Sarkar continued operating, despite government repression, until the period of the 1946 elections.

What the parallel governments demonstrate

These examples show that Quit India was more than a series of demonstrations. In some areas, participants tried to perform functions normally carried out by the colonial state.

However, the examples must be distinguished. Ballia was short-lived, while the parallel administrations at Tamluk and Satara survived for considerably longer periods. Their names, leaders and locations are not interchangeable.

Prelims focus

  • Ballia: United Provinces; Chittu Pandey; August 1942.
  • Tamralipta Jatiya Sarkar: Tamluk, Midnapore, Bengal; established 17 December 1942; associated with Satish Chandra Samanta.
  • Prati Sarkar: Satara, Maharashtra; associated with Nana Patil; developed from 1943.
  • The Satara movement organised people's courts and village volunteer units, including Tufan Dals.
  • Trap: These were local parallel administrations, not 3 independent sovereign states.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, 'Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement', section 'Quit India' and sidebar 'Satara, 1943', printed p. 363; Census of India, District Census Handbook: Ballia, 2011, district historical account of August 1942; Prime Ministers Museum and Library, Manuscript Collections, 'Tamralipta Swadhinata Sangram Itihas Committee', description of the Tamralipta Jatiya Sarkar (consulted 21 November 2026); Press Information Bureau, 'Quit India Movement', 5 August 2017, section on parallel governments (consulted 21 November 2026); Employment News, Vol. 18, 4–10 August 2018, 'Quit India Movement: An Important Milestone in Our Struggle for Freedom', section on local parallel administrations.]

pictures.caption: How local resistance sometimes developed into an alternative administration.

title: Parallel Governments at Ballia, Tamluk and Satara

body:
Why the British response was severe

The Quit India Movement occurred while Britain was fighting the Second World War. The colonial government considered large-scale political unrest a threat to its ability to administer India, maintain communications and conduct wartime operations.

It responded through arrests, restrictions on political organisations, censorship and the use of police and military force. These measures were intended to isolate nationalist organisers and restore government control.

Methods used to suppress the movement

Arrests and detention

The arrest of Gandhi and leading Congress figures on 9 August 1942 was followed by the detention of many other political activists. Congress organisations were restricted or declared unlawful, and numerous local workers were imprisoned.

Control of newspapers and public meetings

Wartime regulations enabled the government to censor political news and restrict public communication. Newspapers faced suppression, while meetings, processions and assemblies could be prohibited.

These measures made open coordination difficult and contributed to the growth of underground communication networks.

Police and military action

Police used lathi charges and firing against demonstrators. Military forces were deployed in affected areas. The government also imposed collective fines in some localities.

Accounts of the suppression record the use of aircraft to fire on crowds in certain places. The intensity of repression varied across districts, but it caused widespread casualties and damaged public confidence in colonial rule.

How extensive was the repression?

By the end of 1943, arrests had reached very large numbers. NCERT's Class 8 history textbook states that over 90,000 people were arrested and around 1,000 people were killed in police firing during the suppression.

These are approximate textbook figures, not a complete or universally agreed count. Other published historical accounts report higher arrest totals. The figures should therefore be understood with their source and reporting period, rather than treated as exact totals accepted by every historical record.

NCERT figures for revision: By the end of 1943, over 90,000 arrests and around 1,000 deaths in police firing. The figures are approximate and relate to the repression of the Quit India Movement.

Why the movement continued despite repression

The initial public upsurge was progressively suppressed in many districts during 1942. Nevertheless, resistance did not end everywhere at the same time. Some activists continued underground work, while local movements and parallel administrations survived into later years.

This difference in duration is important. The mass demonstrations of August 1942, the underground activities that followed, and the longer-running parallel governments formed parts of the same broad movement, but they did not have identical timelines.

Immediate result and historical significance

The Quit India Movement did not immediately end British rule. The British government retained control in 1942, and India became independent only on 15 August 1947, after further wartime developments and political negotiations.

The movement nevertheless had major political significance. It demonstrated the strength of the demand for independence among ordinary Indians and showed that removing prominent national leaders could not necessarily prevent mass political resistance.

It also revealed the limits of colonial authority. In several districts, protest disrupted administration, while underground networks and parallel governments challenged British control in different ways.

The movement is therefore understood as a major phase of the final struggle for independence, rather than as the event that directly transferred power in August 1942.

The essential sequence and relationships

The movement can be understood through a connected sequence. Wartime pressures and the failure of constitutional negotiations led Congress to demand immediate freedom. The August resolution gave that demand an organised national expression. British arrests then produced a largely decentralised uprising, involving public protest, underground work and local alternative administrations. Repression curtailed much of the uprising, but it did not remove the demand for independence.

Prelims focus

  • 8 August 1942: Formal adoption of the Quit India Resolution.
  • 9 August 1942: Arrest of Gandhi and other senior Congress leaders.
  • British repression involved arrests, censorship, police firing and military action.
  • NCERT reports over 90,000 arrests and around 1,000 deaths in police firing by the end of 1943.
  • The movement included mass protest, underground resistance and parallel governments.
  • Trap: Quit India began in 1942; British rule ended in 1947, not immediately after the resolution.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed p. 123; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, 'Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement', section 'Quit India', printed p. 363; Employment News, Vol. 18, 4–10 August 2018, 'Quit India Movement: An Important Milestone in Our Struggle for Freedom', extracts from P. N. Chopra's Quit India Movement, sections on censorship, police repression, casualties and continuing underground resistance; Press Information Bureau, 'Quit India Movement', 5 August 2017 (consulted 21 November 2026).]
